Fuel is a department now, not a button

September 20, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

From the fuel thread on Discord. LtFrosty: “I’m burning 62 mil in fuel each week… I just did a 26 wk contract and it only saves 3.5 mill”, and “it would be cool but probably not realistic if we could purchase our own fuel station, refinery, or trucks.. something to lower the cost”. TheCookiesGuy: “especially as well since they add a premium on top of the percentage so the savings is negligible”. Both were right, and the reason was worse than the symptom: the hedge premium was so large that locking a price was a losing bet on average, whatever the market did. So the correct play was never to hedge — which is exactly what the standings showed. Fuel had one button, and the button was wrong.

  • Hedging is cheaper, longer, and you can get out. Premiums are down by roughly half across the board, there is a new 52-week contract for airlines that want to fix a price for a year, and a live contract can now be unwound early at what it is worth today less a small haircut — so a hedge that has done its job, or one you regret, is no longer something you sit and wait out. A scoreboard on the Fuel tab says what every contract you have ever closed actually made or lost, which is the number the old page never showed you.
  • You can spend money to burn less. Seven fleet-wide efficiency programmes — single-engine taxi, reduced APU use, cost-index flying, engine washes and the rest — each cut burn by a fraction of a percent for a one-off cost and a weekly running charge. Together they are worth about 8%. Each also has a real trade-off: some cost you punctuality, one trades a little margin for fuel, one raises maintenance. Separately, wingtip devices can be retrofitted to individual aircraft from the fleet page for a permanent cut in that tail’s burn and a little extra range.
  • Where you buy the fuel now matters. Every airport has its own fuel price, driven by how close it is to refining and how much competition it has on the ramp — a Gulf hub is cheap, an island station is dear, and the spread is wide enough to change which routes are worth flying. The price is shown on every airport surface in the game: the airport page, the gate table (sortable, so you can rank the world by cheapest fuel), hub management, the route planner, route detail and the airport pickers. Routes can also tanker — carry the return fuel out of the cheaper end — and the game works out every week whether it pays, which it only can when the sector is short enough that the tanks allow it.
  • And you can own the supply. A consortium stake at an airport you fly from makes your fuel there cheaper; a full fuel farm makes it cheaper still, and there is only one farm per airport. Above that sits a refinery: two and a half billion dollars, a year to build, and it moves a fixed slice of your fuel off the jet price and onto crude plus a refining cost. That is not a discount — it is a different bet. When the gap between crude and jet is wide it pays handsomely; when that gap collapses you pay more than the market on every one of those litres and the running costs are due anyway. Delta bought a real one in 2012 for exactly this reason and lost nine figures in the years it went against them. Hedges cannot cover the refined share, because the spread is the thing you bought.

New games start with airport-by-airport fuel pricing on. Existing saves keep flat world fuel and are completely unaffected — every number in a save made before today is what it was.

Two long-standing bugs went out with it. The route planner was forecasting fuel at the normal price no matter what the market was doing, so a route quoted during a spike looked better than it would ever be; it now uses the same fuel number the weekly tick charges. And a malformed hedge could produce a negative fuel bill — that hole is closed.

How hedging works and when it is worth it is in the fuel hedging guide; what fuel does to a route’s economics is in route economics, and burn by type is in the aircraft guide.
